title: Which Item of the Mini Nutritional Assessment–Short Form Predicts In-Hospital Death in Older Patients with Acute Heart Failure? An Item-Level Analysis of the PROFUND-IC Registry
content: Background/Objectives: The Mini Nutritional Assessment–Short Form (MNA-SF) predicts mortality in acute heart failure (AHF), but its score is the sum of six heterogeneous items (food intake, weight loss, mobility, acute stress, neuropsychological status and body mass index [BMI]). Which item carries the prognostic signal is unknown. We aimed to identify the MNA-SF item most predictive of in-hospital death in older patients hospitalised for AHF. Methods: Secondary analysis of the prospective, multicentre PROFUND-IC registry (Spanish internal medicine departments), including patients with complete item-level MNA-SF data at admission. Each item (per 1-point lower score) was related to in-hospital death with Firth-penalised logistic regression (crude, age- and sex-adjusted, and mutually adjusted). Discrimination was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and compared with the total score; ranking stability was assessed by bootstrap. A composite of death or readmission within 365 days was analysed as a secondary outcome with Firth-penalised Cox regression. Results: Of 913 registry patients, 492 were analysed (median age 86.5 [81.1–90.5] years; 293 women); 37 (7.5%) died in hospital. Mobility showed the strongest association (age- and sex-adjusted odds ratio [OR] 2.09 (1.36–3.27); mutually adjusted OR 1.99 (1.27–3.18)) and the only independent one after mutual adjustment. Its AUC (0.67 (0.58–0.75)) was similar to that of the total MNA-SF (0.65 (0.57–0.73); p = 0.774), and it ranked first in 69.0% of bootstrap resamples. BMI, acute stress and neuropsychological problems were not associated with in-hospital death. For the secondary composite (175 events), mobility was again the item most strongly associated (mutually adjusted hazard ratio 1.39 (1.14–1.68)). Conclusions: In older patients with AHF, the prognostic signal of the MNA-SF for in-hospital death is concentrated in its mobility item, a functional rather than strictly nutritional domain. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant external validation.
